summary: Describes base requirements for the Pseudo-Wire Emulation Edge to Edge working group. It guides other documents that define mechanisms for emulating Ethernet, ATM and Frame Relay over packet networks.

plainLanguage.summary: A pseudo-wire carries service data across a packet network between provider-edge devices. This RFC lists what those mechanisms need to do so the service behaves sufficiently like its original circuit.

questions: what does a provider edge device do
subtitle: The requirements for carrying services such as Ethernet, ATM and Frame Relay across packet networks as pseudo-wires.

tldr.problem: Service providers wanted to carry several existing services over a packet network instead of maintaining parallel networks. Customers still expect an emulated service to behave much like its native circuit.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements for encapsulation, frame handling, setup, maintenance, management, service quality and security between provider-edge devices.
tldr.outcome: It guides later service-specific documents but does not define a service or a particular pseudo-wire protocol. TDM requirements are assigned to another document.

facts.label: ATM/Frame Relay checksum
facts.value: Remove at ingress PE and recalculate at egress PE

today: RFC 3916 is an Informational RFC published in September 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements for PWE3 mechanisms rather than defining a particular protocol.

sections.title: Why Emulate Existing Services
sections.content:
Pseudo-Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) emulates essential properties of a service such as ATM, Frame Relay, or Ethernet over a Packet Switched Network (PSN). A customer sees the pseudo-wire as an unshared circuit, though service-specific limitations may prevent some applications from using it.

Providers may operate separate networks for different services, which adds capital, operating, and planning costs. PWE3 requirements are intended to guide mechanisms that let existing services cross a packet-optimized network. The working group standardizes mechanisms, not the services themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: PWE3 carries an existing service over a packet network while aiming to preserve the parts that matter to its users. This RFC gives requirements for building those mechanisms.

sections.title: The PWE3 Reference Model
sections.content:
A pseudo-wire connects two Provider Edge (PE) devices and joins two Attachment Circuits (ACs). Each AC connects a Customer Edge (CE) device to a PE. A PSN may use IP or MPLS, and its tunnel can carry one or more pseudo-wires.

During setup, the PEs are configured or exchange information about the emulated service. A PE encapsulates frames received from its AC and sends them across the pseudo-wire. The remote PE reconstructs the native frames and forwards them to the other CE. A CE is not aware that the service is emulated.
sections.plainLanguage: Each customer device connects to a provider-edge device. The provider-edge devices exchange service data through a pseudo-wire, then deliver reconstructed frames to the other customer device.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Frame Handling
sections.content:
Every PE MUST encapsulate the Protocol Data Units (PDUs) received from an AC, and each PWE3 service MUST specify what its PDU is. The encapsulation must convey information the remote PE needs to process the PDU, support variable lengths where the native service allows them, and provide enough information to separate circuits when trunks are multiplexed.

Each service must specify whether to preserve a frame checksum or remove and recalculate it. For ATM and Frame Relay, the checksum covers link-local circuit identifiers, so it MUST be removed at ingress and recalculated at egress. Services that require ordered delivery MUST provide it; services that disallow duplicates MUST prevent delivery of duplicates. If a payload and its headers exceed the path MTU, the service specification MUST say whether to fragment or drop the frame.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving PE needs enough information to rebuild and route each service frame. Service-specific rules must also cover order, duplicates, checksums, and frames that are too large for the packet path.

sections.title: Setup, Maintenance and Management
sections.content:
Each PWE3 approach MUST define how pseudo-wires are set up and how the PEs exchange required information, such as encapsulation and frame-ordering methods. Setup may be triggered by a management command, an AC event, or auto-discovery; manual configuration is also allowed. A bidirectional circuit can be marked up only when its pseudo-wire and PSN tunnels work in both directions.

In-band native maintenance messages SHOULD pass through unchanged. Each service must define how to handle out-of-band messages. PEs MUST initiate maintenance messages when needed to report faults to CEs, using native-service messages to keep the emulation transparent. Management requirements include SNMP MIBs for circuits and pseudo-wires, statistics, configuration, fault notifications, and connection verification.
sections.plainLanguage: The two provider-edge devices need a defined way to set up a pseudo-wire and agree on how it works. They also need to pass service checks and report failures in a form the customer devices understand.

sections.title: Service Quality, Scope and Security
sections.content:
An emulated service SHOULD resemble its native service, but it is not required to be identical. The applicability statement for each service MUST report limitations. Each CE should see an unshared circuit, be able to define type, speed and MTU when the native service allows it, and receive timely fault notification when the native service would provide it. Service quality need not match the native service; operators decide what quality to provide, and services sensitive to delay or jitter may not suit PWE3.

The working group excludes service interworking, selecting a particular pseudo-wire type, perfect emulation, PSN tunnel signaling, traffic management, and multicast not native to the emulated medium. For security, mechanisms at the pseudo-wire demultiplexer or PSN layer SHOULD protect endpoints and data against denial of service and spoofing. The RFC names IPsec as one possible mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: An emulated circuit should act enough like the original for its intended service, but it may have documented limits in quality or behavior. Security mechanisms should protect the endpoints and tunneled data from spoofing and denial-of-service attacks.
